values.f1:

values.f2: Build for iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, and Linux from one Rust project. Day brings your screens to each platform’s native UI toolkit, with tools for testing, translations, and packaging included.

values.f1:
Rust at the core.
Native on the screen.
values.f2: Write your app in Rust. Give it the controls people already use on their phones and desktops. Day connects the two, so you can share the code while keeping the platform’s native UI.

values.f1:
Your app.
On more devices.
values.f2: A Windows build. An iPhone app. A Linux desktop. Day lets you bring the same Rust project to each, using native controls and shared app logic.

values.f1:
Build it in Rust.
Make it native.
values.f2: Use Rust for the screens as well as the code behind them. Day builds desktop and mobile apps with native UI toolkits and keeps their tests, translations, and release packages in the same project.

fields.text: For Rust developers
fields.html: For Rust developers

fields.text:
Give your Rust code
a native interface.
fields.html: Give your Rust code<br data-astro-cid-lcdefpme="">a native interface.

fields.text: Connect your data models and libraries directly to UI code without crossing language barriers. Compose controls with ordinary functions and attach them to reactive signals that update the interface when data changes.
fields.html: Connect your data models and libraries directly to UI code without crossing language barriers. Compose controls with ordinary functions and attach them to reactive signals that update the interface when data changes.

fields.text: Day uses AppKit on macOS, UIKit on iOS, Material Components on Android, and desktop toolkits on Windows and Linux. Standard controls use toolkit widgets; composed controls and custom drawing have their own implementations. Appearance and capabilities vary by target.
fields.html: Day uses AppKit on macOS, UIKit on iOS, Material Components on Android, and desktop toolkits on Windows and Linux. Standard controls use toolkit widgets; composed controls and custom drawing have their own implementations. Appearance and capabilities vary by target.

fields.text: Explore the Rust API →
fields.html: Explore the Rust API →

fields.text: Reuse your libraries
fields.html: Reuse your libraries

fields.text: Keep parsing, storage, and other app logic in conventional Cargo crates. Use the same code from your UI wherever those crates support the target.
fields.html: Keep parsing, storage, and other app logic in conventional Cargo crates. Use the same code from your UI wherever those crates support the target.

fields.text: Update individual controls
fields.html: Update individual controls

fields.text: Bindings update existing controls when their signals change. Adding or replacing a screen can create new controls; ordinary value updates do not require rebuilding the whole interface.
fields.html: Bindings update existing controls when their signals change. Adding or replacing a screen can create new controls; ordinary value updates do not require rebuilding the whole interface.

fields.text: Compile to native machine code
fields.html: Compile to native machine code

fields.text: Your Rust code compiles to machine code for each desktop and mobile target, alongside Day’s native toolkit integrations.
fields.html: Your Rust code compiles to machine code for each desktop and mobile target, alongside Day’s native toolkit integrations.

values.f1: The UI is Rust code
values.f2: A screen is a function returning impl Piece. Compose controls with function calls, configure them with builder methods, and attach closures to events. Your UI can call the same Cargo crates as the rest of the app.
values.f3: Day uses AppKit on macOS, UIKit on iOS, Material Components on Android, and desktop toolkits on Windows and Linux. Standard controls use native widgets; composed controls and custom drawing have separate implementations. Appearance and capabilities vary by target.
values.f6: Call your parsing, storage, and other Rust libraries from the UI. Check that their dependencies support each target you plan to ship.
values.f8: A signal change reruns the bindings that read it and updates the affected controls. Value changes don’t rebuild the whole UI; structural changes can create or remove controls.
values.f10: Rust compiles your code to machine code for each desktop and mobile target, alongside Day’s toolkit integrations.

values.f1: Use the platform’s controls
values.f2: A Day text field on macOS is an AppKit text field. Its editing and selection behavior come from the toolkit. Your Rust code handles the app’s data and what happens when someone uses the control.
values.f3: The other targets work with their platform toolkits, including UIKit and Android’s Material Components. Standard controls use toolkit widgets. Composed controls and custom drawing vary by implementation, so check the controls your app needs on each target.
values.f6: Use Cargo crates for the app’s data model and libraries. The UI calls that code on the targets its dependencies support.
values.f8: Signals notify the bindings that use them. Updating a label’s value keeps the existing control; replacing a screen can build new ones.
values.f10: Each desktop or mobile build contains compiled Rust code and the native toolkit integration for that target.

values.f1: Change the state. Update the control.
values.f2: Bind a label to a counter and update the counter in a button’s closure. Day updates the label when the value changes. The function that built the screen doesn’t have to run again.
values.f3: Controls connect to AppKit, UIKit, Material Components, and the desktop toolkits on Windows and Linux. Standard widgets get their behavior from those toolkits. Composed controls and custom drawing have separate implementations, with differences between targets.
values.f6: App logic stays in Cargo crates. Reuse your libraries wherever they and their dependencies support the target.
values.f8: Signal bindings update existing controls. Structural operations, such as replacing a page, can build and dispose subtrees.
values.f10: Rust produces machine code for your desktop and mobile targets, built alongside Day’s platform integrations.

values.f1: Write the screen in the language you use
values.f2: Use functions for components, closures for event handlers, and signals for changing values. The screens and the rest of your app can share Rust types and call the same libraries.
values.f3: Day connects that code to AppKit, UIKit, Material Components, and the desktop toolkits on Windows and Linux. Standard controls use native widgets. Custom drawing and composed controls have separate implementations; expect some differences in appearance and capability.
values.f6: Keep data handling and storage in Cargo crates and call them from the UI. Verify their dependencies on each target.
values.f8: Bindings rerun when the signals they read change. An ordinary value update doesn’t rebuild the screen; adding or replacing UI can create controls.
values.f10: Rust compiles to native machine code for each target. Day’s toolkit integrations are built with the app.
